title: Thousands of servers can be backdoored by exploiting buggy motherboard controllers
gist: Black Hat research by runZero's HD Moore found over a dozen new BMC (baseboard management controller) vulnerabilities across HPE, Supermicro, Dell, Lenovo, Huawei and others, with scans showing 54% of 86,000 internet-exposed BMCs and 29% of 126,761 internally-scanned BMCs carrying critical flaws — evidence that datacenter out-of-band management remains a chronically under-patched attack surface more than a decade after the risk was first flagged.

insights.claim: An external Internet scan by HD Moore found more than 86,000 baseboard management controllers (BMCs) exposing a management service to the public, and over 54 percent of those devices contained one or more critical vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: More than half of publicly exposed enterprise server management interfaces are critically vulnerable, meaning a large, discoverable pool of high-value backdoor targets exists right now — a concrete metric for cyber-risk exposure at scale across the server hardware supply chain.

insights.claim: A separate internal scan of 126,761 BMCs inside corporate networks found nearly 29 percent had one or more critical vulnerabilities.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Even behind the firewall, roughly 1 in 3 BMCs is critically vulnerable, meaning perimeter security alone does not neutralize this risk class — relevant for enterprise security budget allocation toward internal network segmentation.

insights.claim: As many as 75,000 of the internet-exposed BMCs remained vulnerable to CVE-2013-4786, a 13-year-old flaw in the IPMI 2.0 authentication protocol that enables offline cracking of administrator-level BMC account passwords.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A vulnerability publicly known since 2013 still affecting ~87% of exposed BMCs demonstrates a structural patching failure in the server hardware ecosystem, not a one-off bug — a durable, systemic risk rather than a transient news event.

insights.claim: Moore, CEO and founder of security firm runZero, uncovered more than a dozen new vulnerabilities in BMCs sold by HPE, Supermicro, Avocent, Huawei, Lenovo, Dell, and others, spanning authentication-handshake bypasses, unenforced encryption in-session, predictable session tokens, pre-authentication memory corruption, unsigned firmware, extractable hardcoded secrets, and weak factory-default credentials.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Seven bug classes spanning nearly every major server OEM means the risk is systemic to the BMC hardware category, not isolated to one vendor — investors evaluating hardware/infrastructure security vendors (runZero, Eclypsium, etc.) or datacenter operators should note this as a durable market for firmware security tooling.
insights.locator: A vulnerability list that grows by the day

insights.claim: HPE's factory-randomized default BMC passwords were found to be the weakest among vendors tested (eight digits or alphanumeric), while Supermicro and Dell use slightly longer defaults that raise the cost and time required for offline password cracking.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A vendor-level ranking of default-credential strength is directly actionable for security teams prioritizing which server fleets need urgent credential rotation, and is a reputational/liability data point for HPE specifically.
insights.locator: A vulnerability list that grows by the day

insights.claim: The two most significant predictable-session-identifier vulnerabilities Moore found, which allow attackers to hijack live BMC sessions across both IPMI and browser-based KVM consoles, are both present in Supermicro systems.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Supermicro appears repeatedly across multiple bug classes in this research (session hijacking, unsigned firmware, extractable secrets), suggesting its BMC implementation carries disproportionate risk relative to peers — relevant for enterprises and cloud buyers doing vendor risk assessment.
insights.locator: A vulnerability list that grows by the day

themes.theme: Precedent: BMC exploitation is not hypothetical

insights.claim: In 2021, researchers discovered ILObleed, a malicious implant that infected HPE servers with wiper firmware destroying stored data; the implant survived OS reinstalls and hard drive swaps and would reactivate the disk-wiping attack, exploiting a vulnerability that had been patched in HPE BMCs four years earlier but never installed on the compromised devices.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: This is a real, prior-confirmed case of BMC-level compromise causing catastrophic, persistence-resistant data loss — proof that the newly disclosed vulnerability classes are not theoretical and that unpatched BMC firmware is an active liability for any HPE server fleet operator.
insights.locator: A vulnerability list that grows by the day

insights.claim: Last year, the US Cybersecurity and Infrastructure Security Agency (CISA) added a critical vulnerability in an AMI BMC to its Known Exploited Vulnerabilities list.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: Federal regulators are already treating BMC vulnerabilities as actively exploited in the wild, which raises the likelihood of compliance mandates (e.g., federal procurement requirements) forcing faster BMC patching across the industry.
insights.locator: A vulnerability list that grows by the day

insights.claim: Moore is keeping most new vulnerability details confidential until BMC makers have time to patch them, and has released an open source scanning tool called OOBscan that lets administrators detect the growing catalog of BMC vulnerabilities across their server fleets.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A free open-source detection tool lowers the barrier for enterprises to audit BMC risk immediately, and its adoption rate could become a rough proxy for how seriously the industry is responding to this disclosure.
insights.locator: A vulnerability list that grows by the day

insights.claim: Moore's recommended mitigations include setting long unique usernames and complex passwords, disabling IPMI wherever possible, disabling KCS to block host-side BMC access, and isolating each BMC network interface individually rather than sharing a VLAN.
insights.speaker: Dan Goodin
insights.so_what: A concrete, low-cost mitigation checklist that datacenter and cloud operators can implement immediately without waiting for vendor patches, reducing near-term exploitation risk.
insights.quote: BMCs are still an underrated risk. This work points to the ecosystem being well behind the curve in terms of code quality and architecture.
